title: "Instruction Tuning"
description: "Fine-tuning a model on examples that demonstrate how to follow instructions."
term: "Instruction Tuning"
letter: "I"
category: "LLM Engineering"
difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

Instruction tuning trains a language model on examples of instructions and
helpful responses. It teaches the model to respond to requests in a desired
format or style, rather than only continuing text in the way its original
training encouraged.

## Technical explanation

Instruction tuning is commonly implemented as supervised fine-tuning on
prompt-response examples. The examples can cover tasks, formats, and
domains; their quality and diversity influence the resulting behavior. It
is one stage in model adaptation and is distinct from supplying instructions
in a prompt at inference time.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Instruction-tuned models are easier to use in assistants and task-oriented
applications because they are more likely to treat natural-language
requests as directions. Tuning data, evaluation, and safety testing still
need to reflect the model's intended users and deployment context.

## How it works

Training examples pair an instruction, sometimes with additional context,
with a target response. The model generates the response tokens, and a
training objective adjusts its parameters to increase the likelihood of
those targets. Some systems follow this stage with preference-based or
other alignment training.

## Practical example

A model can be fine-tuned on examples that ask it to summarize a passage
in three bullet points. The resulting model may follow that format more
reliably, but should still be tested on unseen passages and instructions.

## Common misconceptions

- Instruction tuning changes model parameters; adding an instruction to a
  prompt does not.
- Tuning does not guarantee that a model will follow every instruction
  correctly or safely.
- More examples are not automatically better if they are low quality,
  repetitive, or inconsistent.
